title: The first pledge of Aqaba
hook: twelve pledge not to steal, lie, kill their children or slander

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yathrib, and six strangers who sat and heard him. Your line was: six listened.

A year goes by. The pilgrimage comes round again, and so do the men from Yathrib: twelve of them this time, Ibn Ishaq says. They meet the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, at the same spot, Aqaba, a narrow pass on the edge of Mina, away from the crowds. They've had a year at home to talk, to argue, to wonder. Now they've come back with their hands out. Not to ask for anything. To give their word. Today: the first pledge of Aqaba.
screen: `A YEAR LATER.` → `TWELVE COME BACK.` → `HANDS OUT TO PLEDGE.`

segments.voice: What did they promise? Ubada ibn al-Samit, whom the sirah names among the twelve, gives the terms in Sahih al-Bukhari. The Prophet said: pledge to me that you will not set up any partner with God, that you will not steal, that you will not commit adultery, that you will not kill your children, that you will not bring a slander you have invented between your hands and feet, and that you will not disobey me in what is right. Whoever keeps it, his reward is with God. Look at that list. No army, no money, no promise to fight for anyone. It's about how they will live: their hands, their tongues, their homes, their children. Ibn Ishaq says this kind of pledge came to be called the pledge of women, and that it carried no promise of war. The Qur'an, in surah sixty, describes believing women pledging much the same things to the Prophet. And there's a mercy built in. In Ubada's report the Prophet adds: whoever falls into any of these and is punished in this world, that is an expiation. And whoever falls and God covers it, it is up to God, to forgive or to punish. The pledge is clear, and realistic. It expects people to be tested, and it doesn't throw them away when they stumble. The twelve go home carrying a promise about conduct. Not yet a promise of protection. That comes later.
screen: `NO PARTNER WITH GOD.` · `NO STEALING, NO SLANDER.` · `NO ARMY, NO MONEY.` · `ROOM FOR THOSE WHO STUMBLE.` · then, large: `A PLEDGE OF CONDUCT.`

segments.voice: The twelve didn't promise to be good in general; they named things. So name one line you want to keep, from the story's list or your own, and say it to yourself in a single plain sentence, the kind you could actually keep. If you pray, you can place it before God.
Aqaba, the narrow pass where twelve men of Yathrib pledged the Prophet a way of living, not a war. Today's word.
Your line: a pledge of conduct. Clear enough to keep, with room for anyone who stumbles. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims remember the first pledge of Aqaba as a promise about how to live, and the same list of conduct appears in the Qur'an's description of women pledging to the Prophet.

chat.says: What did the first Muslims from Medina actually promise the Prophet at Aqaba?
options: A way of living: no partner with God, no theft, no adultery, no slander.
To fight beside him against Mecca whenever he called on them.
To hand him a share of their harvest and trade every year.
chat.meaning: Ubada's report lists rules of conduct, and Ibn Ishaq says this first pledge carried no promise of war.

Ubada ibn al-Samit.meaning: named among the twelve; he reported the pledge's terms

Mina.meaning: a valley near Mecca, on the pilgrims' route

sirah.meaning: the story of the Prophet's life

Sahih al-Bukhari.meaning: a major collection of the Prophet's sayings

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 18 (Ubada ibn al-Samit: the terms of the pledge; punishment in this world as expiation; if God covers it, it is up to Him)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (twelve men at Aqaba the following year; the 'pledge of women', with no obligation to fight)
Qur'an 60:12 (the pledge of the believing women)

notes: Count of twelve and 'a year later' are from Ibn Ishaq; confirm.
Bukhari 18 cited for Ubada's report; some readers link Bukhari 18 to the first Aqaba pledge, others to a later pledge. Confirm the attribution and number.
Terms paraphrased from Ubada's report; index hook says 'lie', the report says slander; written to the report.
Aqaba described as 'a narrow pass on the edge of Mina'; confirm.

Editor pass: Ubada is now 'named among the twelve in the sirah' rather than flatly 'one of the twelve' telling it, since Bukhari 18's link to the first Aqaba is debated; the 'pledge of women' line no longer states a reason Ibn Ishaq does not give, and the Qur'an 60:12 parallel is put as a separate, softer sentence.
Audit pass: checked against Bukhari 18 and Ibn Ishaq's pledge-of-women line; no change.
